root.meaning: to put cattle out to pasture

stages.meaning: to earn; to win, to take by force

history: When you gagner your salary, you are, by origin, grazing cattle. The Frankish verb *waidanjan meant ‘to put animals out to pasture’, and it is related to German Weide, ‘pasture’. In French the meaning moved to ‘to cultivate the land’, probably, says the TLFi, because of crop rotation: a field that had been pasture was then ploughed and sown. From farming the word moved to what farming brings in. Around 1135, written gaaignier, it already meant both ‘to earn’ and ‘to win, to take by force’. Both senses are alive today: gagner sa vie, ‘to earn a living’, and gagner un match, ‘to win a match’. The old farming sense survived in dialects of eastern France.
historyEinfach: Gagner comes from Frankish, the language of the Franks. Their verb meant ‘to let animals eat grass’. In old French it meant ‘to work the land’. From the land, people got food and money. So gagner came to mean ‘to earn’, and also ‘to win’: gagner de l'argent, gagner un match.

elsewhere.text: German Weide, a pasture, comes from the same Germanic root as the Frankish verb behind gagner.
